props.title: Anatomy of a Murder
props.initialSlug: Lawyer defends killer with bold "irresistible impulse"

sections.content: Anatomy of a Murder (1959) revolutionized the courtroom drama with its groundbreaking frankness about sexual assault and murder. Director Otto Preminger challenged the Production Code by using terms like "rape" and "sexual penetration" - unprecedented for 1959. James Stewart delivers one of his finest performances as Paul Biegler, a small-town lawyer defending an army lieutenant accused of murder. The film's raw authenticity comes from real-life judge Joseph N. Welch playing the presiding judge, and its attention to actual legal procedure influenced everything from To Kill a Mockingbird (1962) to A Few Good Men (1992).

sections.content: What sets Anatomy of a Murder apart is its morally ambiguous territory. Unlike To Kill a Mockingbird (1962), where the innocence of Tom Robinson is clear, Preminger keeps us guessing about Lieutenant Manion's guilt. The film suggests that legal truth isn't about actual innocence but what can be proven in court. This cynical view influenced later films like ...And Justice for All (1979) and Primal Fear (1996), where the legal system itself becomes a character of questionable morality.

Duke Ellington's jazz score marks another innovation - the first Hollywood film scored entirely by an African American composer. This musical choice adds a layer of sophistication and unpredictability that matches the film's complex moral landscape. The score influenced later courtroom dramas like Philadelphia (1993) and Chicago (2002) to use music as commentary on legal proceedings. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

movies.title: Judgment at Nuremberg
movies.slug: Stanley Kramer's powerful drama about the Nazi war crime trials features exceptional performances from Spencer Tracy and Maximilian Schell.

sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond courtroom dramas. Its documentary-like attention to procedure inspired Sidney Lumet's police procedurals like Serpico (1973) and Prince of the City (1981). The way it handles adult themes within the constraints of the Production Code created a template for serious adult dramas that directors like Stanley Kubrick would follow with films like Lolita (1962).
